summary: Winged burning bush is a shrub that spreads by forming dense thickets that crowd out and shade other plants. Each plant produces more than 100 seeds that birds and small animals carry to new locations far away. While it typically grows in disturbed areas, it can also establish itself in natural areas that have few other invasive plants.
history: Winged euonymus is native to Asia and arrived in the region through the landscaping industry, where it was sold as an ornamental shrub. The plant also spread when people discarded floral arrangements containing its fruit. In New York, this species is regulated, meaning it can still be sold but cannot be intentionally released into the wild.

handling.text: Some local infestations cover up to 3 acres. Its seeds can stay alive for up to two years, so removal needs follow-up for several years. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
